ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: An $8\mathrm{~m}$ long rope is fastened to the corner of the house. A dog is fastened to the rope. Find the perimeter of the area where the dog can be found.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure there is a rectangular house, the top is marked 6 m, the left side is marked 4 m; an 8 m long rope is tied to the upper-left corner of the house, and the dog is on the left side of the house. Then reason: Taking the tying point as the center of the circle, the house blocks one quadrant in the lower right, so the rope can first sweep out an arc with radius 8 and central angle 270°, and the arc length is (3/4)·2π·8 = 12π. If the rope winds around to the upper-right corner, along the top side it has first used 6 m, leaving 2 m, so at the upper-right corner it can still form an arc with radius 2 and central angle 90°, and the arc length is (1/4)·2π·2 = π. If the rope winds around to the lower-left corner, along the left side it has first used 4 m, leaving 4 m, so at the lower-left corner it can still form an arc with radius 4 and central angle 90°, and the arc length is (1/4)·2π·4 = 2π. From the lower-right corner to the tying point, whether going along the top side and then down, or first along the bottom side and then across, both require 6+4=10 m, exceeding 8 m, so it cannot reach the lower-right corner. The straight-line parts on the boundary come from the outside edges of the house: top side 6 m, left side 4 m, reachable right side 2 m, reachable bottom side 4 m, totaling 16. The total perimeter is 12π + π + 2π + 16 = 15π + 16.

method.method_draft: Directly trace the boundary of the dog’s reachable region. From the image, identify the house as a rectangle with the rope tied at the upper-left corner, top side labeled 6 m and left side labeled 4 m. From the text, use rope length 8 m. The dog can first sweep a 270-degree arc of radius 8 around the tied corner, since the house blocks one quadrant. If the rope wraps around the upper-right corner, 6 m of rope is used along the top edge, leaving 2 m, giving a 90-degree arc of radius 2. If the rope wraps around the lower-left corner, 4 m is used along the left edge, leaving 4 m, giving a 90-degree arc of radius 4. The rope cannot reach the lower-right corner because either route requires 10 m before any remaining rope. Add arc lengths: (3/4)(2π·8) + (1/4)(2π·2) + (1/4)(2π·4) = 12π + π + 2π = 15π. Then add the straight wall portions that form part of the perimeter of the accessible region: top edge 6, left edge 4, reachable part of right edge 2, and reachable part of bottom edge 4, totaling 16. Therefore the perimeter is 15π + 16.

method.method_draft: Use a corner-state or shortest-path-around-obstacle model. From the image, label the tied upper-left corner A, the upper-right corner B, the lower-left corner D, and the lower-right corner C of the rectangular house, with AB = 6 m and AD = 4 m. From the text, the total rope length is 8 m. For each corner that the rope can pivot around, compute the residual rope length after reaching it along the house boundary. At A, residual length is 8 and the exposed angular measure is 270 degrees, producing arc length 12π. At B, the shortest path from A is 6, leaving residual 2, and only the outside quarter around B is newly exposed, producing arc length π. At D, the shortest path from A is 4, leaving residual 4, and the outside quarter around D is newly exposed, producing arc length 2π. At C, the shortest path from A is 6 + 4 = 10, which exceeds 8, so no arc centered at C is possible. Next determine the straight boundary intervals on the obstacle itself reachable by these corner states: AB contributes 6, AD contributes 4, the right side from B contributes 2, and the bottom side from D contributes 4, for a total straight length of 16. Add the circular contributions 15π and straight contributions 16 to get 15π + 16.
